key_insight: As the compression-ramp angle increases and the shock/boundary-layer interaction strengthens, wall-pressure fluctuations and acoustic loading rise dramatically, with the largest loads appearing downstream of reattachment rather than at the shock foot.
engineering_relevance: This matters for hypersonic vehicle design because ramp geometry can strongly amplify unsteady pressure and acoustic loads, affecting structural integrity, thermal protection, and sensor placement.
method: Large-eddy simulations at Mach 6.04 with inlet momentum-thickness Reynolds number Reθ = 4340.
Compression-corner angles tested: 10°, 20°, 30°, and 34°, spanning attached to strongly separated flow regimes.
Pressure, spectra, and band-isolated acoustic-loading maps were analyzed to separate turbulence, low-frequency motion, and shock-associated fluctuations.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 312% increase in peak RMS wall-pressure from R20 to R30 and another 67% from R30 to R34, with acoustic loading rising from 140 dB upstream to about 177 dB downstream of reattachment in the 34° case.
watch_item: The results are from one Mach/Reθ condition and a limited set of ramp angles, so extrapolation to other hypersonic configurations or real-flight boundary conditions should be done cautiously.
paper_title: Acoustic Loading Beneath High-Speed Flow Over a Compression Ramp at Different Angles
